0%

孫子 (Sun Tzu)

1 mindset · 18 decision rules · 1 algorithm

孫子, personal name 孫武, courtesy name 長卿, was a military man from 齊 (Qi), traditionally placed in the late Spring and Autumn period (544–496 BC). The earliest account of his life is Sima Qian's biography in 《史記·孫武孫臏吳起列傳》, written around 97 BC — roughly500 years after he is supposed to have lived; in it吳王闔廬 says 「子之十三篇，吾盡觀之矣」 ("your thirteen chapters — I have read them all") before testing him by drilling the king's 180 concubines, which he then turns into a functioning unit by executing the two company commanders who laughed (史記/卷065, Wikisource (https://zh.wikisource.org/wiki/%E5%8F%B2%E8%A8%98/%E5%8D%B7065)). The biography credits him with 「西破彊楚，入郢，北威齊晉」 — breaking Chu, entering Ying, overawing Qi and Jin — a claim Sima Qian attaches to 孫子 and to no one else's strategy. What is known of his actual decisions is almost entirely the text 《孫子兵法》, thirteen chapters that open by declaring war 「國之大事，死生之地，存亡之道」 and never stop being an argument about how to decide under that weight (孫子兵法, 始計第一 (https://zh.wikisource.org/wiki/%E5%AD%AB%E5%AD%90%E5%85%B5%E6%B3%95)). That text's earliest layer is generally dated by scholars to the Warring States period, at least a century after the Sun Wu of the 《史記》 — Song-dynasty scholar 葉世 first noticed that the much earlier 《左傳》 never mentions him (Sun Tzu, Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun_Tzu)). The 1972 excavation of the銀雀山 Han tomb near Linyi, Shandong, turned up a Western Han bamboo copy of thirteen fragmentary chapters of 《孫子》 plus five further pieces under other or lost titles, alongside the then-lost 《孫臏兵法》 — the oldest physical witness to his writing (Yinqueshan Han Slips (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yinqueshan_Han_Slips)). The honest summary: a man whose recorded biography is one famous training episode and one claimed campaign, and whose recorded reasoning is unusually complete and unusually early.

From the first research round; its Chinese quotes were checked, its other facts were not re-checked.

algorithm

Reckon before battle

Before fighting, lay the war out by five matters (the Way, heaven, ground, the general, law) and compare the two sides on seven questions. Whoever comes out ahead in the reckoning before battle wins, whoever has less does not, and having none is worse still. A second passage gives the reckoning as an ordered chain: the ground gives measurement, measurement gives quantity, quantity gives number, number gives the weighing of the sides, and the weighing gives victory.

「兵者，國之大事，死生之地，存亡之道，不可不察也。故經之以五事，校之以七計，而索其情：一曰道，二曰天，三曰地，四曰將，五曰法。」…「道者，令民與上同意，可與之死，可與之生，而不畏危也。」…「故校之以七計而索其情，曰：主孰有道？將孰有能？天地孰得？法令孰行？兵眾孰強？士卒孰練？賞罰孰明？吾以此知勝負矣。」…「夫未戰而廟算勝者，得算多也；未戰而廟算不勝者，得算少也。多算勝，少算不勝，而況於無算乎？」 — "War is a great matter of state, the ground of life and death, the way to survival or ruin; it must be examined. So lay it out by five matters, compare it by seven reckonings, and search out the true situation: the Way, heaven, ground, the general, law… The Way is what makes the people one in intent with their superior, so that they will die with him or live with him and not fear danger… Compare by the seven reckonings: Which ruler has the Way? Which general has ability? Who has heaven and ground? Whose laws and orders are carried out? Whose troops are stronger? Whose officers and men are better trained? Whose rewards and punishments are clearer? By this I know victory and defeat… One who wins the temple reckoning before battle has gained more 算; one who does not has gained fewer. More wins, fewer does not, how much less none at all?" 「兵法：一曰度，二曰量，三曰數，四曰稱，五曰勝。地生度，度生量，量生數，數生稱，稱生勝。故勝兵若以鎰稱銖，敗兵若以銖稱鎰。」 — "In the method of war: first measurement, second quantity, third number, fourth weighing, fifth victory. Ground gives rise to measurement, measurement to quantity, quantity to number, number to weighing, weighing to victory. So a winning army is like a yi weighed against a zhu, a losing army like a zhu against a yi."

《孫子兵法》始計第一 (l.12–18); 軍形第四 (l.59).

quoted

decision rule

Make yourself unbeatable first; win, then seek battle

First make yourself unbeatable, then wait for the enemy to become beatable. Being unbeatable is in your own hands, being beatable is in the enemy's, and you cannot make the enemy certain to be beatable; so the winning army wins first and then seeks battle. Do not rely on the enemy not coming or not attacking; rely on having the means to meet them and on having what cannot be attacked.

「昔之善戰者，先為不可勝，以待敵之可勝。不可勝在己，可勝在敵。故善戰者，能為不可勝，不能使敵之必可勝。故曰：勝可知，而不可為。」…「古之所謂善戰者，勝於易勝者也。」…「故善戰者，立於不敗之地，而不失敵之敗也。是故勝兵先勝而後求戰，敗兵先戰而後求勝。」 — "The skilled fighters of old first made themselves unbeatable and waited for the enemy to become beatable. Being unbeatable lies with oneself; being beatable lies with the enemy. So the skilled fighter can make himself unbeatable but cannot make the enemy certain to be beatable. Hence: victory can be known but cannot be made… Those the ancients called skilled fighters won where winning was easy… The skilled fighter stands where he cannot be defeated and does not miss the enemy's defeat. So the winning army wins first and then seeks battle; the losing army fights first and then seeks victory." 「故用兵之法，無恃其不來，恃吾有以待之；無恃其不攻，恃吾有所不可攻也。」 — "Do not rely on their not coming; rely on having the means to meet them. Do not rely on their not attacking; rely on having what cannot be attacked."

軍形第四 (l.51, l.57); 九變第八 (l.109).

quoted

decision rule

Whole over broken; strike plans first, walled cities last

Prefer keeping things whole to breaking them, at every scale from the state to the five-man squad. Subduing the other side's army without battle is the best of the best; a hundred victories in a hundred battles is not. Rank the targets as follows: plans highest, then alliances, then armies, and attacking walled cities lowest, as the method for when there is no alternative.

「凡用兵之法，全國為上，破國次之；全軍為上，破軍次之；全旅為上，破旅次之；全卒為上，破卒次之；全伍為上，破伍次之。是故百戰百勝，非善之善者也；不戰而屈人之兵，善之善者也。故上兵伐謀，其次伐交，其次伐兵，其下攻城。攻城之法，為不得已。修櫓轒轀，具器械，三月而後成；距闉，又三月而後已。將不勝其忿，而蟻附之，殺士三分之一，而城不拔者，此攻之災也。故善用兵者，屈人之兵而非戰也，拔人之城而非攻也，毀人之國而非久也，必以全爭於天下，故兵不頓而利可全，此謀攻之法也。」 — "In using troops, a whole state is best, a broken one next; a whole army best, a broken one next; and so for brigade, company and squad. So a hundred victories in a hundred battles is not the best of the best; to subdue the other's army without battle is the best of the best. So the highest use of troops strikes plans, the next strikes alliances, the next strikes troops, the lowest attacks walled cities. Attacking cities is the method for when there is no alternative: three months to make shields, assault carts and equipment, three more for the earthen mounds; if the general cannot master his anger and sends the men swarming up like ants, a third of them are killed and the city still stands — this is the calamity of attack. So the skilled user of troops subdues the other's army without battle, takes the other's city without attacking it, destroys the other's state without a long war; he contends for all under heaven by keeping things whole, so his troops are not blunted and the gain can be whole."

謀攻第三 (l.34–38).

quoted

decision rule

Know whether you can fight; know the other side and yourself

  • Five things tell you who will win:
    • knowing when you can and cannot fight;
    • knowing how to use large and small forces;
    • superiors and subordinates wanting the same thing;
    • being prepared and waiting for the unprepared;
    • an able general whom the ruler does not interfere with.
  • Knowing the other side and yourself, a hundred battles hold no danger. Knowing yourself but not them, you win one and lose one. Knowing neither, every battle is dangerous.
  • Knowing whether your troops can attack and whether the enemy can be attacked, but not whether the ground permits battle, is still only half a victory.

「故知勝有五：知可以戰與不可以戰者勝，識衆寡之用者勝，上下同欲者勝，以虞待不虞者勝，將能而君不御者勝。此五者，知勝之道也。故曰：知彼知己，百戰不殆；不知彼而知己，一勝一負；不知彼不知己，每戰必殆。」 — "There are five ways to know victory: one who knows when he can fight and when he cannot wins; one who knows how to use many and few wins; one whose superiors and subordinates want the same thing wins; one who, prepared, waits for the unprepared wins; one whose general is able and whose ruler does not interfere wins. These five are the way to know victory. Hence: know the other and know yourself, and in a hundred battles you are not in danger; not knowing the other but knowing yourself, one win, one loss; knowing neither, in every battle you are in danger." 「知吾卒之可以擊，而不知敵之不可擊，勝之半也；知敵之可擊，而不知吾卒之不可以擊，勝之半也；知敵之可擊，知吾卒之可以擊，而不知地形之不可以戰，勝之半也。…故曰：知彼知己，勝乃不殆；知天知地，勝乃可全。」 — "Knowing our troops can attack but not that the enemy cannot be attacked is half a victory; knowing the enemy can be attacked but not that our troops cannot attack is half a victory; knowing the enemy can be attacked and our troops can attack, but not that the ground does not permit battle, is half a victory… Hence: know the other and yourself, and victory is not in danger; know heaven and ground, and victory can be whole."

謀攻第三 (l.46–48); 地形第十 (l.135).

quoted

decision rule

Move only when it accords with advantage; never from anger

Do not move without advantage, do not use troops without gain, do not fight unless in danger; a ruler must not raise an army out of anger, nor a general give battle out of resentment. Move when it accords with advantage and stop when it does not. Anger can turn back into joy, but a destroyed state cannot be restored and the dead cannot be brought back.

「夫戰勝攻取，而不修其功者凶，命曰『費留』。故曰：明主慮之，良將修之，非利不動，非得不用，非危不戰。主不可以怒而興師，將不可以慍而致戰。合於利而動，不合於利而止。怒可以復喜，慍可以復悅，亡國不可以復存，死者不可以復生。故明主慎之，良將警之，此安國全軍之道也。」 — "To win battles and take objectives without 修 the achievement is ill-omened; it is called 費留. Hence the enlightened ruler considers it and the good general attends to it: do not move without advantage, do not use troops without gain, do not fight unless in danger. A ruler must not raise an army out of anger; a general must not give battle out of resentment. Move when it accords with advantage; stop when it does not. Anger can become joy again, resentment can become pleasure again; a destroyed state cannot exist again, the dead cannot live again. So the enlightened ruler is careful of it and the good general is wary of it: this is the way to keep the state secure and the army whole." On 修 and 費留, the commentators split; see Changes #8. The same gate is in 九地: 「合於利而動，不合於利而止。」 The bamboo 〈見吳王〉 gives the same stance in dialogue. It is in English only here; I did not open a Chinese transcription. Ames translates: "Using the military is to gain the advantage; it is not a matter of being fond of it… it is not a matter of sport."

火攻第十二 (l.159); 九地第十一 (l.140). For 〈見吳王〉: Roger T. Ames, Sun-tzu: The Art of Warfare (Ballantine, 1993), Part II ch.5, from the 1985 銀雀山 edition.

quoted (火攻, 九地). The 〈見吳王〉 line is attributed: it is a narrated dialogue, and Ames judges that both it and the 史記 drill story are later than the core text.

mindset

In deliberating, mix harm into benefit

The wise always mix benefit and harm together when they deliberate. With benefit mixed in, the undertaking can be carried out; with harm mixed in, trouble can be resolved. Whoever does not fully know the harm of using troops cannot fully know its benefit.

「是故智者之慮，必雜於利害，雜於利而務可信也，雜於害而患可解也。」 — "So the wise one's deliberation always mixes benefit and harm: mixed with benefit, the undertaking can be carried out (杜牧: 「信，申也」); mixed with harm, trouble can be resolved." 「故不盡知用兵之害者，則不能盡知用兵之利也。」 — "Whoever does not fully know the harm of using troops cannot fully know its benefit."

九變第八 (l.107); 作戰第二 (l.21).

quoted

decision rule

War is the way of deception

War is the way of deception:

  • When able, appear unable; when using troops, appear not to; when near, appear far; when far, appear near.
  • Act on the enemy's condition: lure, take in disorder, prepare against the solid, avoid the strong, provoke the angry, make the humble arrogant, tire the rested, split the close-knit.
  • Attack where they are unprepared, and come out where they do not expect.

War stands on deceit, moves by advantage, and changes by dividing and combining.

「兵者，詭道也。故能而示之不能，用而示之不用，近而示之遠，遠而示之近。利而誘之，亂而取之，實而備之，強而避之，怒而撓之，卑而驕之，佚而勞之，親而離之。攻其無備，出其不意。此兵家之勝，不可先傳也。」 — "War is the way of deception. So when able, show inability; when using, show non-use; when near, show far; when far, show near. With advantage, lure them; in disorder, take them; solid, prepare against them; strong, avoid them; angry, stir them; humble, make them arrogant; rested, tire them; close, separate them. Attack where they are unprepared; come out where they do not expect. These are the strategist's victories; they cannot be handed down in advance." 「故兵以詐立，以利動，以分合為變者也。」 — "So war is established by deceit, moved by advantage, and varied by dividing and combining."

始計第一 (l.16); 軍爭第七 (l.96).

quoted

decision rule

Value victory, not duration; speed; supply from the enemy

In war, value victory and not duration. A long campaign blunts the troops, exhausts strength and leaves the state short, and no state has ever benefited from a long war: clumsy speed is heard of, skilful prolongation has never been seen. Do not levy twice or haul grain three times; take provisions from the enemy, for one measure of his grain equals twenty of one's own.

「凡用兵之法，馳車千駟，革車千乘，帶甲十萬，千里饋糧，…日費千金，然後十萬之師舉矣。其用戰也，貴勝，久則鈍兵挫銳，攻城則力屈，久暴師則國用不足。…故兵聞拙速，未睹巧之久也。夫兵久而國利者，未之有也。」…「善用兵者，役不再籍，糧不三載；取用於國，因糧於敵，故軍食可足也。」…「故智將務食於敵，食敵一鍾，當吾二十鍾。」…「故兵貴勝，不貴久。」 — "A thousand fast chariots, a thousand armoured carts, a hundred thousand armoured men, grain carried a thousand li… a thousand gold a day, and only then can an army of a hundred thousand be raised. In using it to fight, value victory: long, and it blunts the troops and dulls their edge; attacking cities, strength is spent; the army long in the field, the state's means fall short… So in war one hears of clumsy speed, but has not seen skill that is prolonged. A long war that benefits the state has never been… The skilled user of troops does not levy twice nor haul grain three times; he takes equipment from his own state and provisions from the enemy, so the army's food is enough… So the wise general strives to eat from the enemy: one zhong of the enemy's food equals twenty of mine… So in war value victory, not duration." 「故兵之情主速，乘人之不及，由不虞之道，攻其所不戒也。」 — "The nature of war is to rely on speed: take advantage of the other's not being in time, go by roads they do not anticipate, attack where they are not on guard."

作戰第二 (l.21, 23, 27, 31); 九地第十一 (l.140).

quoted

decision rule

Bring the other side to you; do not be brought

Whoever is first on the field and awaits the enemy is fresh; whoever comes later and hurries into battle is weary. So the skilled fighter brings others and is not brought by them: he draws them with advantage and keeps them off with harm.

  • When he wants battle, he attacks what they must rescue.
  • When he does not, he diverts them from their course.
  • Against a large, ordered enemy, he first seizes what they cherish, and they comply.

「凡先處戰地而待敵者佚，後處戰地而趨戰者勞。故善戰者，致人而不致於人。能使敵自至者，利之也；能使敵不得至者，害之也。」…「故我欲戰，敵雖高壘深溝，不得不與我戰者，攻其所必救也；我不欲戰，雖畫地而守之，敵不得與我戰者，乖其所之也。」 — "Whoever occupies the field first and awaits the enemy is at ease; whoever occupies it later and hurries to battle is weary. So the skilled fighter brings others and is not brought by others. What makes the enemy come of himself is advantage; what keeps him from coming is harm… When I want battle, though the enemy has high walls and deep moats, he must fight me, because I attack what he must rescue; when I do not want battle, though I only draw a line on the ground and hold it, he cannot fight me, because I divert him from where he is going." 「敢問：敵衆整而將來，待之若何？曰：先奪其所愛，則聽矣。」 — "May I ask: the enemy, many and in order, is about to come; how do I meet him? Answer: first seize what he cherishes, and he will comply."

虛實第六 (l.75–81); 九地第十一 (l.140).

quoted

decision rule

Avoid the solid, strike the empty; have no constant form

Make the enemy show its form while you show none: then you are concentrated and they are divided, and an enemy that prepares everywhere is thin everywhere. Like water, which avoids the high and runs to the low, an army avoids the solid, strikes the empty and shapes its victory by the enemy. It has no fixed 勢 and no constant form, and its victories are not repeated.

「故形人而我無形，則我專而敵分。…無所不備，則無所不寡。寡者，備人者也；衆者，使人備己者也。」…「人皆知我所以勝之形，而莫知吾所以制勝之形。故其戰勝不復，而應形於無窮。」…「夫兵形象水，水之行，避高而趨下；兵之勝，避實而擊虛。水因地而制行，兵因敵而制勝。故兵無成勢，無恒形，能因敵變化而取勝者，謂之神。」 — "So I make others take form while I have none; then I am concentrated and the enemy divided… Preparing everywhere, he is few everywhere. Being few is preparing against others; being many is making others prepare against you… Everyone knows the form by which I won, but no one knows the form by which I controlled the victory. So the victories are not repeated, and the response to forms is without end… The army's form is like water: water in its course avoids the high and hastens to the low; an army in its victory avoids the solid and strikes the empty. Water shapes its course by the ground; an army shapes its victory by the enemy. So an army has no fixed 勢 and no constant form; one who can take victory by changing with the enemy is called divine."

虛實第六 (l.83, 87, 89).

quoted

decision rule

Foreknowledge must come from people; pay for it

Foreknowledge cannot be had from spirits, from likeness to past events, or from measurement; it must be got from people who know the enemy's situation. It is the height of inhumanity to keep a war going for years, at a ruinous daily cost, for a victory decided in one day, yet grudge ranks, salaries and a hundred pieces of gold and so not know the enemy's situation. Of the five kinds of spy, knowledge rests on the converted spy, so he must be treated most generously.

「凡興師十萬，出征千里，百姓之費，公家之奉，日費千金，…相守數年，以爭一日之勝，而愛爵祿百金，不知敵之情者，不仁之至也，非人之將也，非主之佐也，非勝之主也。故明君賢將，所以動而勝人，成功出於眾者，先知也。先知者，不可取於鬼神，不可象於事，不可驗於度，必取於人，知敵之情者也。」…「五間之事，主必知之，知之必在於反間，故反間不可不厚也。」 — "Raising a hundred thousand and marching a thousand li, the people's spending and the state's outlay come to a thousand gold a day… To hold out for several years to contend for one day's victory, yet begrudge ranks, salaries and a hundred gold and so not know the enemy's situation, is the height of inhumanity: no general of men, no aid to a ruler, no master of victory. What lets the enlightened ruler and the wise general move and defeat others, with achievements beyond the crowd, is foreknowledge. Foreknowledge cannot be taken from ghosts and spirits, cannot be got by analogy with events, cannot be verified by measurement (度; 李筌: 「度，數也」); it must be taken from people who know the enemy's situation… The ruler must know the work of the five kinds of spy; knowing it rests on the converted spy, so the converted spy must be treated generously."

用間第十三 (l.162, 168).

quoted

decision rule

Seek it in 勢, made of the regular and the irregular, not from the people

Battle 勢 is no more than the regular (正) and the irregular (奇): engage with the regular, win with the irregular, and their combinations cannot be exhausted. The skilled fighter seeks victory in 勢 and does not demand it of his people, so he can choose his people and rely on 勢; courage and cowardice are a matter of 勢.

「三軍之衆，可使必受敵而無敗者，奇正是也。」…「凡戰者，以正合，以奇勝。…戰勢不過奇正，奇正之變，不可勝窮也。奇正相生，如循環之無端，孰能窮之哉？」…「勇怯，勢也」…「故善戰者，求之於勢，不責於人，故能擇人而任勢。任勢者，其戰人也，如轉木石。木石之性，安則靜，危則動，方則止，圓則行。」 — "That the whole army can take the enemy's attack without defeat is the work of 奇 and 正… In all battle, engage with the regular and win with the irregular… The 勢 of battle are no more than irregular and regular, yet their changes cannot all be exhausted. Irregular and regular give rise to each other like a ring without end; who can exhaust them?… Courage and cowardice are a matter of 勢… So the skilled fighter seeks it in 勢 and does not demand it of people; so he can choose people and rely on 勢. One who relies on 勢 fights with men as one rolls logs and stones: by nature logs and stones are still on level ground and move on a slope; square, they stop; round, they roll." 勢 is defined in 始計 as 「勢者，因利而制權也」: "勢 is shaping one's leverage by advantage."

兵勢第五 (l.62, 64, 68, 72); 始計第一 (l.16).

quoted

decision rule

Not every road is taken, and not every command of the ruler is accepted

There are roads not to be taken, armies not to be struck, cities not to be attacked, ground not to be contested, and commands of the ruler not to be accepted. When the way of battle means sure victory and the ruler says do not fight, fighting is permissible; when it means no victory and the ruler says fight, not fighting is permissible. The general advances without seeking fame and retreats without avoiding blame, protecting only the people.

「途有所不由，軍有所不擊，城有所不攻，地有所不爭，君命有所不受。」 — "There are roads one does not take, armies one does not strike, cities one does not attack, ground one does not contest, ruler's commands one does not accept." 「故戰道必勝，主曰無戰，必戰可也；戰道不勝，主曰必戰，無戰可也。是故進不求名，退不避罪，唯民是保，而利合於主，國之寶也。」 — "So when the way of battle means sure victory, though the ruler says do not fight, fighting is permissible; when the way of battle does not mean victory, though the ruler says fight, not fighting is permissible. So one who advances not seeking fame and retreats not avoiding blame, protecting only the people and whose gain accords with the ruler's, is the treasure of the state." 謀攻 names three ways the ruler brings trouble on his army: 「不知軍之不可以進而謂之進，不知軍之不可以退而謂之退，是為縻軍；不知三軍之事，而同三軍之政，則軍士惑矣；不知三軍之權，而同三軍之任，則軍士疑矣。」 — "ordering advance or retreat without knowing whether the army can, which is hobbling the army; sharing in the army's administration without knowing its affairs, which confuses the soldiers; sharing in its command without knowing its expedients, which makes them doubt." The 史記 drill story shows him acting on this: 「臣既已受命為將，將在軍，君命有所不受。」 — "Having received the command as general, while the general is with the army there are commands of the ruler he does not accept." The bamboo 〈四變〉 explains the clause. It is in English only here (Ames): "That there are commands from the ruler not to be obeyed means that if the commands of the ruler are contrary to these four contingencies, do not obey them."

九變第八 (l.105); 地形第十 (l.131); 謀攻第三 (l.44); 《史記》卷六十五 孫子吳起列傳 (l.13); 〈四變〉 in Ames 1993, Part II ch.2.

quoted (九變, 地形, 謀攻). The 史記 line is attributed (司馬遷's narrative). 〈四變〉 is attributed: Ames reads it as commentary on the core text.

decision rule

Choose the action by the ratio of forces

With ten to one, surround; five to one, attack; two to one, divide; equal, you can fight; fewer, you can hold (a variant reads "slip away"); outmatched, you can avoid. A small force that holds stubbornly is taken by a large one. Numbers are not valued for their own sake: it is enough not to advance recklessly, to concentrate strength, size up the enemy and take men, and whoever lacks forethought and slights the enemy is sure to be captured.

「故用兵之法，十則圍之，五則攻之，倍則分之，敵則能戰之，少則能守之，不若則能避之。故小敵之堅，大敵之擒也。」 — "So in using troops: ten to one, surround them; five to one, attack them; double, divide them; equal, be able to fight them; fewer, be able to hold; not a match, be able to avoid them. So the stubbornness of a small force is the capture of a large one." 「故兵非貴益多也，惟無武進，足以併力、料敵、取人而已。夫惟無慮而易敵者，必擒於人。」 — "So in war more is not what is valued; only do not advance rashly; enough to combine strength, size up the enemy and take men. Only one who lacks forethought and slights the enemy is sure to be captured by others." Readings differ:

  • 十一家注 reads 「少則能逃之」.
  • On 倍則分之, 曹操 reads "divide your own force into regular and irregular" (「以二敵一，則一術爲正，一術爲奇」), 王晳 reads it as splitting into two forces so the enemy is hit front and back, and 陳皥 as sending part of the force at what the enemy must rescue, so that the enemy divides.
  • Ames 1993 (n.125) swaps the 倍 and 敵 clauses by emendation.

謀攻第三 (l.40); 行軍第九 (l.122); 十一家注孫子·謀攻篇 (Wikisource).

quoted

decision rule

The general's faults: five dangers, six defeats

Examine the general for five dangers, each a handle for the enemy:

  • one set on dying can be killed;
  • one set on living can be captured;
  • the quick-tempered can be provoked by insult;
  • the scrupulous about honour can be shamed;
  • one who loves the people can be harried.

The six kinds of defeat (flight, slackness, sinking, collapse, disorder, rout) are not disasters from heaven but the general's faults, and the text names the cause of each.

「故將有五危︰必死，可殺也﹔必生，可虜也﹔忿速，可侮也﹔廉潔，可辱也﹔愛民，可煩也。凡此五者，將之過也，用兵之災也。覆軍殺將，必以五危，不可不察也。」 — "The general has five dangers: set on dying, he can be killed; set on living, he can be captured; quick to anger, he can be insulted; scrupulous, he can be shamed; loving the people, he can be troubled. These five are the general's faults, the calamities of using troops. The overturned army and the slain general come from the five dangers; they must be examined." 「故兵有走者、有弛者、有陷者、有崩者、有亂者、有北者。凡此六者，非天之災，將之過也。夫勢均，以一擊十，曰走；卒强吏弱，曰弛；吏强卒弱，曰陷；大吏怒而不服，遇敵懟而自戰，將不知其能，曰崩；將弱不嚴，教道不明，吏卒無常，陳兵縱橫，曰亂；將不能料敵，以少合衆，以弱擊強，兵無選鋒，曰北。」 — "Armies have flight, slackness, sinking, collapse, disorder and rout. These six are not calamities from heaven but the general's faults. With 勢 equal, striking ten with one is flight; strong men and weak officers is slackness; strong officers and weak men is sinking; senior officers angry and insubordinate, fighting on their own from resentment when they meet the enemy, with the general not knowing their ability, is collapse; a weak, lax general, unclear instruction, officers and men without constancy and ranks every which way is disorder; a general who cannot size up the enemy, meets many with few and strong with weak, and has no picked vanguard, is rout."

九變第八 (l.111); 地形第十 (l.129).

quoted

decision rule

Orders clear first, then enforced; care that cannot command is useless

If orders are not clear and not drilled in, it is the general's fault; if they are clear and still not followed, it is the officers' fault. Punish troops before they are attached to you and they will not submit, but once they are attached, if punishment is not carried out, they cannot be used. Care without the power to direct and command makes soldiers like spoiled children: useless.

「約束不明，申令不熟，將之罪也；既已明而不如法者，吏士之罪也。」 — "If the rules are not clear and the orders not made familiar, it is the general's fault; if they are already clear and are not followed as the law requires, it is the officers' fault." In the story he says the first sentence alone after the first failure, then repeats the orders before the second. The bamboo 〈見吳王〉 has the same rule. It is in English only here (Ames): "If one does not order them, or if one's orders are not understood, it is the fault of the commander. If one has already issued orders and has explained them, it is the fault of the field officers." 「卒未親附而罰之，則不服，不服則難用也。卒已親附而罰不行，則不可用也。故令之以文，齊之以武，是謂必取。」 — "Punish soldiers before they are attached and they will not submit, and if they do not submit they are hard to use. Once they are attached, if punishment is not carried out, they cannot be used. So command them with civility and keep them uniform with martial discipline: this is called sure success." 「視卒如嬰兒，故可以與之赴深溪；視卒如愛子，故可與之俱死。厚而不能使，愛而不能令，亂而不能治，譬若驕子，不可用也。」 — "Regard the soldiers as infants and they will go into deep valleys with you; regard them as beloved sons and they will die with you. Generous but unable to direct, loving but unable to command, disorderly and unable to control: they are like spoiled children, of no use."

《史記》卷六十五 (l.13); 〈見吳王〉 in Ames 1993, Part II ch.5; 行軍第九 (l.124); 地形第十 (l.133).

The 史記 and 〈見吳王〉 lines are attributed: narrated, and per Ames both versions are later than the core text. The 行軍 and 地形 lines are quoted.

decision rule

Learn the enemy by probing and by signs

Learn the enemy by acting on him:

  • reckon him (策) to know the gains and losses of his plans;
  • stir him (作) to learn the pattern of his movement and stillness;
  • make him take form (形) to know his ground of life and death;
  • test him in contact (角) to know where he has more and where less.

Read his intent from what can be seen. Humble words with more preparation mean he will advance; strong words with a forward push mean he will withdraw; asking for peace without a pledge means a plot; half advancing and half withdrawing means a lure. The chapter lists many more signs.

「故策之而知得失之計，作之而知動靜之理，形之而知死生之地，角之而知有餘不足之處。」 — "So reckon them to know the calculation of gain and loss; stir them to know the pattern of movement and stillness; give them form to know the ground of death and life; test them to know where there is surplus and shortage." 「敵近而靜者，恃其險也；遠而挑戰者，欲人之進也；…辭卑而益備者，進也；辭強而進驅者，退也；…無約而請和者，謀也；…半進半退者，誘也；杖而立者，饑也；…見利而不進者，勞也；鳥集者，虛也；夜呼者，恐也；軍擾者，將不重也；旌旗動者，亂也；吏怒者，倦也；…數賞者，窘也；數罰者，困也。」 — "Near and quiet: they rely on their strong ground. Far off and challenging: they want you to advance… Humble words and more preparation: they will advance. Strong words and pressing forward: they will withdraw… Asking for peace without a pledge: a plot… Half advancing, half withdrawing: a lure. Leaning on their weapons as they stand: hungry… Seeing advantage and not advancing: weary. Birds gathering: the camp is empty. Calling out at night: afraid. The camp in uproar: the general lacks weight. Banners moving: disorder. Officers angry: exhausted… Frequent rewards: in straits. Frequent punishments: in distress."

虛實第六 (l.87); 行軍第九 (l.120).

quoted

decision rule

Spirit, heart, strength and change: meet theirs with yours

An army's spirit can be taken and a general's heart can be taken. Four management rules follow:

  • Managing spirit: avoid the enemy's spirit when it is keen, and strike when it flags and turns homeward.
  • Managing the heart: await disorder with order, and clamour with calm.
  • Managing strength: await the far-come while near, the weary while rested, the hungry while fed.
  • Managing change: do not intercept well-ordered banners or strike an imposing array.

Eight prescriptions:

  1. 1. Do not attack up a high hill.
  2. 2. Do not meet head-on an enemy with a hill at its back.
  3. 3. Do not follow a feigned flight.
  4. 4. Do not attack crack troops.
  5. 5. Do not take bait.
  6. 6. Do not block an army going home.
  7. 7. Leave a gap for a surrounded army.
  8. 8. Do not press a desperate enemy.

「三軍可奪氣，將軍可奪心。是故朝氣銳，晝氣惰，暮氣歸。故善用兵者，避其銳氣，擊其惰歸，此治氣者也；以治待亂，以靜待嘩，此治心者也；以近待遠，以佚待勞，以飽待饑，此治力者也；無邀正正之旗，無擊堂堂之陣，此治變者也。」 — "The army's spirit can be taken; the general's heart can be taken. So morning spirit is keen, midday spirit slack, evening spirit turns homeward. So the skilled user of troops avoids keen spirit and strikes the slack and homeward: this is managing spirit. With order await disorder, with stillness await clamour: this is managing the heart. Near, await the distant; at ease, await the weary; fed, await the hungry: this is managing strength. Do not intercept orderly banners, do not strike an imposing array: this is managing change." 「故用兵之法，高陵勿向，背丘勿逆，佯北勿從，銳卒勿攻，餌兵勿食，歸師勿遏，圍師必闕，窮寇勿迫，此用兵之法也。」 — "So the method of using troops: a high hill, do not face up it; a hill at their back, do not oppose; feigned flight, do not follow; crack troops, do not attack; bait troops, do not swallow; an army going home, do not block; a surrounded army, always leave a gap; a desperate enemy, do not press." The commentators read 朝/晝/暮 two ways: 杜牧 takes them as times of day, while 孟氏, 梅堯臣 and 王晳 take them as the start, middle and end of a campaign.

軍爭第七 (l.100, 102); 十一家注孫子·軍爭篇.

quoted

decision rule

Name the ground, act as prescribed; troops with no way out fight

Identify the ground by the conditions the chapter defines, then act as prescribed:

  • scattered ground: do not fight;
  • light ground: do not halt;
  • contested ground: do not attack;
  • open-crossing ground: do not get cut off;
  • crossroads ground: join allies;
  • heavy ground: plunder;
  • broken ground: keep moving;
  • enclosed ground: use stratagem;
  • dead ground: fight.

Troops deep in hostile land with nowhere to go fight to the death without being ordered. The chapter says the variations of the nine grounds and the pattern of human feelings must be examined.

「是故散地則無戰，輕地則無止，爭地則無攻，交地則無絕，衢地則合交，重地則掠，圮地則行，圍地則謀，死地則戰。」 — "So on scattered ground, do not fight; on light ground, do not halt; on contested ground, do not attack; on crossing ground, do not be cut off; on crossroads ground, join in alliances; on heavy ground, plunder; on broken ground, keep going; on enclosed ground, scheme; on dead ground, fight." (Each ground is defined in l.138, e.g. 「疾戰則存，不疾戰則亡者，為死地」 — "ground where you survive if you fight fast and perish if you do not is dead ground.") 「投之無所往，死且不北。死焉不得，士人盡力。兵士甚陷則不懼，無所往則固，深入則拘，不得已則鬥。」…「投之亡地然後存，陷之死地然後生。夫衆陷於害，然後能為勝敗。」…「九地之變，屈伸之利，人情之理，不可不察也。」 — "Throw them where there is nowhere to go and they will die rather than flee; facing death, what can they not achieve? Officers and men give their full strength. Soldiers deeply trapped do not fear; with nowhere to go they hold firm; deep in, they cling together; with no choice, they fight… Throw them into ground where they would perish, and they survive; sink them into dead ground, and they live. Only when the mass has fallen into harm can it decide victory or defeat… The variations of the nine grounds, the advantage of drawing in or extending, the pattern of human feelings: these must be examined." The same chapter gives a second list for each ground of what the commander himself does (「散地，吾將一其志…死地，吾將示之以不活」, l.148).

九地第十一 (l.138, 142, 146, 148, 150).

quoted

decision rule

Which house falls first: judge by the land unit, the tax, and what they breed

The King of Wu asked which of the six houses dividing Jin would fall first. Sunzi named Fan and Zhonghang first, then Zhi, then Han and Wei, while Zhao, keeping its old laws, would hold and Jin would go to it. His reason, given house by house (Ames's translation), had two sides:

  • The houses that fell: small land units plus the tax gave full coffers and many officials, so the ruler grew arrogant and the ministers wasteful, and they fought often for exploits.
  • Zhao: the largest unit and no new taxes gave empty coffers and few officials, a frugal ruler and humble ministers over a prosperous people, so it held.

「吴王问孙子曰："六将军分守晋国之地，孰先亡、孰固成？"孙子曰："范、中行是(氏)先亡。""孰为之次？""智是(氏)为次。""孰为之次？""韩魏为次，赵毋失其故法，晋国归焉。"」 (simplified characters, as printed by 何炳棣) — "The King of Wu asked Master Sun: 'Of the six commanders who divided and held the land of Jin, which will perish first, and which will hold firm?' Master Sun said: 'Fan and Zhonghang will perish first.' 'Who next?' 'Zhi next.' 'Who next?' 'Han and Wei next. Zhao has not lost its old laws, and the state of Jin will go to it.'" The reasoning is in English only here (Ames): "Fan and Chung-hang took eighty square paces as a yuan, and took one hundred and sixty square paces as a chen, and then made five households their basic tax unit. The land area was small and the officials in office were many. With five households as the basic tax unit, the public coffers prospered. With the public coffers prospering and the officials in office many, the ruler became arrogant and his ministers wasteful. And in pursuit of great exploits they embarked on frequent wars. Thus I say they were the first to perish… Chao took one hundred and twenty square paces as a yuan, and took two hundred and forty square paces as a chen, and so there were no new taxes forthcoming for the public coffers. With the public coffers empty and the officials in office few, the ruler was frugal and his ministers humble in their management of what was a prosperous people. Thus I say that he held on to his lands." The closing line is the king's, not Sunzi's: 「王者之道明矣，厚爱其民者也」 — "The way of the true king is clear: it is to love his people generously."

銀雀山漢簡〈吳問〉. Chinese as quoted in 何炳棣〈中國現存最古的私家著述《孫子兵法》〉 (https://www.aisixiang.com/data/101665.html). English from Ames 1993, Part II ch.1 and n.230. Ames reads 伍稅 as "five households as the tax unit"; 何炳棣, in his own words rather than the slips', describes Fan and Zhonghang as 「亩最小，税最重」 (smallest unit, heaviest tax).

attributed (a narrated dialogue in the bamboo text)

0%

老子 (Laozi)

5 mindsets · 13 decision rules · 1 algorithm

Almost nothing about the historical person is known, and the earliest source says so itself. Sima Qian's 《史記·老子韓非列傳》 (vol. 63, c. 1st century BCE — roughly 500 years after the period in question) is the first biography: 老子者，楚苦縣厲鄉曲仁里人也，姓李氏，名耳，字耼，周守藏室之史也 — a keeper of the Zhou royal archive. His entire recorded life is two episodes: Confucius, then51, travelling to Zhou to ask him about ritual, and his own departure west when he saw Zhou declining, writing two parts of a little over 5,000 characters at the gatekeeper Yin Xi's request. Sima Qian does not even claim to have the right man: he offers three candidates (李耳, 老萊子, 太史儋) and writes 或曰儋即老子，或曰非也，世莫知其然否 — "or it was him, or it was not; the world does not know whether it is so." The ages he reports (百有六十餘歲，或言二百餘歲) are plainly legendary, and his ending is 莫知其所終 — nobody knows where he ended. No inscription, letter, state record or contemporary text of Laozi survives. The book is worse attested than the man: Sima Qian describes it as two undivided parts with no chapters, and the 81-chapter divisions and chapter titles are a later editorial layer (Wang Bi, 3rd century CE, and the 河上公 tradition) that scholars still argue about — 姚鼐 argued in 1783 that they were arbitrary cuts. The excavated manuscripts show the text still growing: Guodian (c. 300 BCE) preserves only about 31 of the received 81 chapters, in a different order, with none of chapters 70–81; the earliest complete version is the Mawangdui silk manuscript (c. 168 BCE). So the decision rules below are, strictly, the rules of a text of uncertain authorship compiled over centuries — with one exception, Rule 2, the only words anywhere recorded as Laozi actually advising someone.

From the first research round; its Chinese quotes were checked, its other facts were not re-checked.

algorithm

Take away, and take away again.

Learning adds something every day; the Way takes something away every day. Take away, and take away again, until you reach not-doing (無為); with not-doing, nothing is left undone.

為學日益，為道日損。損之又損，以至於無為。無為而無不為。取天下常以無事，及其有事，不足以取天下。 — "Pursuing learning, one gains daily; pursuing the Way, one loses daily. Lose and lose again, until one arrives at not-doing. Not doing, and nothing is left undone. The world is always taken by having no business; once one has business, one is not enough to take the world." Guodian 乙: 学者日益，为道者日员（损）。员（损）之或员（损），以至亡为也，亡为而亡不为。 — "The learner gains daily; the one who does the Way loses daily. Lose and again lose, until not-doing; not-doing, and nothing not done."

道德經 ch. 48 (王弼本, sources/lao-tzu/道德經__王弼本_.txt); 郭店 乙 slips 3–4 (zh.wikisource 郭店楚墓竹簡). Silk B (zh.wikisource 老子 (帛書本), received ch. 48) has 為學者日益，聞道者日云﹦之有云，以至於無□□□□□□□□□□取天下恆無事… — "聞道者" (one who hears the Way), and a lacuna where the formula would be. The 取天下 sentence is in WB and silk B but not in Guodian, whose slip runs straight on to 絕學亡憂.

quoted

decision rule

Know what is enough; know to stop.

Know what is enough and you are not disgraced; know to stop and you are not endangered, and can last long. No calamity is greater than not knowing what is enough.

名與身孰親？身與貨孰多？得與亡孰病？是故甚愛必大費，多藏必厚亡，知足不辱，知止不殆，可以長久。 — "Name or self: which is dearer? Self or goods: which counts for more? Gaining or losing: which is the sickness? So great fondness must mean great expense, and much hoarding must mean heavy loss. Knowing what is enough, one is not disgraced; knowing to stop, one is not endangered; one can last long." (ch. 44) · 禍莫大於不知足；咎莫大於欲得。故知足之足，常足矣。 — "No calamity is greater than not knowing what is enough; no fault is greater than wanting to get. So the enough of knowing enough is a lasting enough." (ch. 46) · 始制有名，名亦既有，夫亦將知止，知止所以不殆。 — "When ordering begins there are names; once there are names, one will also know to stop; knowing to stop is how one is not endangered." (ch. 32) Guodian 甲: 古（故）智（知）足不辱，智（知）止不怠（殆），可以长旧（久）。 (ch. 44) · 化（祸）莫大○（乎）不智（知）足。智（知）足之为足，此亘（恒）足矣。 (ch. 46) · 夫亦○（将）智（知）止，智（知）止所以不○（殆）。 (ch. 32)

道德經 chs. 44, 46, 32 (王弼本); 郭店 甲 35–37 (ch. 44), 5–6 (ch. 46), 19–20 (ch. 32); silk ch. 7 = received 44 (silk.txt:87; silk A also preserves the line).

quoted

decision rule

Stop before it is full; when the work is done, withdraw.

Holding something and filling it to the brim is not as good as stopping. When the work is done, withdraw yourself; that is the Way of heaven. Accomplish and do not settle in it; because one does not settle in it, it does not leave.

持而盈之，不如其已；揣而梲之，不可長保。金玉滿堂，莫之能守；富貴而驕，自遺其咎。功遂身退，天之道。 — "To hold it and fill it is not as good as stopping. Hammer it to a point and it cannot be kept long. Gold and jade fill the hall and none can guard them. Rich, high and arrogant, one brings blame on oneself. The work done, the self withdraws: this is the Way of heaven." (ch. 9) · 功成而弗居。夫唯弗居，是以不去。 — "The work is achieved and he does not dwell in it. Just because he does not dwell in it, it does not leave." (ch. 2) Guodian 甲: ○而○（盈）之，不不若已。…攻（功）述（遂）身退，天之道也。 (ch. 9) · 成而弗居。天〈夫〉唯弗居也，是以弗去也。 (ch. 2)

道德經 chs. 9 and 2 (王弼本); 郭店 甲 37–39 (ch. 9), 17–18 (ch. 2). Silk B has 功遂身退，天之道也 and silk A has 功遂身芮 (帛書本 page); the 校勘版 prints 功述身芮 (silk.txt:567).

quoted

decision rule

Acting on it ruins it; gripping it loses it.

Whoever acts on it ruins it and whoever grips it loses it, so the sage does not act and does not ruin, does not grip and does not lose. The world is a sacred vessel that cannot be acted on, so the sage drops the extreme, the extravagant and the excessive.

為者敗之，執者失之。是以聖人無為故無敗，無執故無失。 — "One who acts on it spoils it; one who holds on to it loses it. So the sage does not act, and therefore does not spoil; does not hold, and therefore does not lose." (ch. 64) · 將欲取天下而為之，吾見其不得已。天下神器，不可為也，為者敗之，執者失之。…是以聖人去甚，去奢，去泰。 — "One who wants to take the world and act on it: I see that he will not get it. The world is a sacred vessel; it cannot be acted on. One who acts on it spoils it; one who holds it loses it. … So the sage discards the extreme, the extravagant, the excessive." (ch. 29) Guodian 甲: 为之者败之，执之者远之。是以圣人亡为古（故）亡败；亡执古（故）亡○（失）。 ("one who holds it pushes it away") · Guodian 丙: 为之者败之，执之者○（失）之。

道德經 chs. 64 and 29 (王弼本); 郭店 甲 10–11, 丙 11 (ch. 64; ch. 29 is not in Guodian). Silk ch. 73 = received 29 (silk.txt:795–801) has 夫天下 神器也 非可為者也 … 去甚 去大 去楮 (silk B: 去諸).

quoted

decision rule

I do not act, and the people transform by themselves.

Govern a state with the straight, use troops with the unexpected, and take the world by having no business. The sage says: I do not act and the people transform by themselves; I like stillness and the people set themselves right; I have no business and the people grow rich by themselves; I have no desires (Guodian and silk: "I want not to want") and the people become simple by themselves.

以正治國，以奇用兵，以無事取天下。…故聖人云：「我無為而民自化，我好靜而民自正，我無事而民自富，我無欲而民自樸。」 — "Govern the state with the straight, use troops with the unexpected, take the world with no business. … So the sage says: 'I do not act, and the people transform themselves; I love stillness, and the people correct themselves; I have no business, and the people enrich themselves; I have no desire, and the people become plain by themselves.'" (ch. 57) · 道常無為而無不為。侯王若能守之，萬物將自化。 — "The Way constantly does not act, and yet nothing is left undone. If lords and kings can keep to it, the ten thousand things will transform by themselves." (ch. 37) Guodian 甲: 以正之（治）邦，以○（奇）○（用）兵，以亡事取天下。…是以圣人之言曰：我无事而民自○（富）。我亡为而民自○（化）。我好青（静）而民自正。我谷（欲）不谷（欲）而民自朴。 (ch. 57) · ○（道）亘（恒）亡为也，侯王能守之，而万勿（物）○（将）自○（化）。 (ch. 37)

道德經 chs. 57 and 37 (王弼本); 郭店 甲 29–32 (ch. 57), 13 (ch. 37); silk ch. 20 = received 57 (silk.txt:216–220). At ch. 37 Guodian has 道恆亡為也 with no 而無不為, and both silk copies have 道恆無名 with no 無為 (帛書本 page; silk.txt:891).

quoted

decision rule

Act while it is small and easy; treat it as difficult.

What is at rest is easy to hold and what has shown no sign is easy to plan for, so act on a thing before it exists and put it in order before it is in disorder. Taking many things as easy brings many difficulties, so the sage still treats them as difficult and in the end has no difficulty.

其安易持，其未兆易謀。其脆易泮，其微易散。為之於未有，治之於未亂。合抱之木，生於毫末；九層之臺，起於累土；千里之行，始於足下。 — "What is at rest is easy to hold; what has not yet shown a sign is easy to plan for. What is brittle is easy to split; what is minute is easy to scatter. Act on it before it exists; order it before it is in disorder. A tree a man's arms can circle grows from a hair-tip; a nine-storey terrace rises from piled earth; a thousand-li journey begins under the feet." (ch. 64) · 圖難於其易，為大於其細；天下難事必作於易，天下大事必作於細。是以聖人終不為大，故能成其大。夫輕諾必寡信，多易必多難。是以聖人猶難之，故終無難矣 — "Plan for the difficult while it is easy; do the great while it is small. The world's difficult affairs must arise from the easy, its great affairs from the small. So the sage never does the great, and therefore can achieve the great. Light promises must bring little trust; much taken as easy must bring much difficulty. So the sage still treats things as difficult, and therefore in the end has no difficulty." (ch. 63) Guodian 甲: 其安也，易○也。其未○（兆）也，易○（谋）也。其○（脆）也，易畔（判）也。其几也，易○（散）也。为之于其亡又（有）也。○（治）之于其未乱。合□□□□□□□，九成之台甲□□□□□□□□□足下。 (ch. 64) · 为亡为，事亡事，未（味）亡未（味）。大少（小）之多惕（易）必多○（难）。是以圣人猷（犹）○（难）之，古（故）终亡○（难）。 (ch. 63)

道德經 chs. 64 and 63 (王弼本); 郭店 甲 25–27 (ch. 64), 14–15 (ch. 63). Guodian's ch. 63 lacks 圖難於其易, 天下難事必作於易 and 輕諾必寡信; silk A has them (silk.txt:284–290). The images differ by witness. WB has 九層之臺，起於累土；千里之行. Silk A has 九成之臺作於羸土，百仁（仞）之高台（始）於…, and silk B …作於欙土，百千之高始於足[下]. Guodian is broken at that point. "A journey of a thousand li" appears in WB only among these witnesses.

quoted

decision rule

Be as careful at the end as at the beginning.

People in their affairs often fail when the work is nearly done; be as careful at the end as at the beginning, and no affair fails.

民之從事，常於幾成而敗之。慎終如始，則無敗事。 — "People, in their undertakings, often fail when they are close to finishing. Careful at the end as at the beginning: then no undertaking fails." (ch. 64) Guodian 甲: 临事之纪，誓（慎）冬（终）女（如）○（始），此亡败事矣。 — "The rule (紀) for approaching an affair: careful at the end as at the start. Then there is no failed affair." Guodian 丙: ○（慎）终若○（始），则无败事喜（矣）。人之败也，亘（恒）于其○（且）成也败之。 — "…People's failing always comes when they are about to succeed."

道德經 ch. 64 (王弼本); 郭店 甲 11, 丙 12; silk ch. 27 (silk.txt:299).

quoted

decision rule

Know that you do not know.

To know that you do not know is best. The second clause is a sickness, but the witnesses differ on its wording: silk A says "not knowing that you do not know", while WB and silk B have 不知知, whose sense is disputed. Only by treating the sickness as a sickness is one not sick; the sage is not sick because he treats the sickness as a sickness.

知不知上，不知知病。夫唯病病，是以不病。聖人不病，以其病病，是以不病。 — "Knowing not-knowing: highest. Not-knowing knowing: sickness. Only by treating sickness as sickness is one not sick. The sage is not sick because he treats sickness as sickness; therefore he is not sick." (WB) · Silk A: 知不知尚矣，不﹦知﹦病矣 (= 不知不知，病矣 — "not knowing that one does not know is a sickness"). Silk B: 知不知尚矣，不知﹦病矣 (= 不知知，病矣, as WB). Wang Bi's commentary on the clause, not main text: 不知知之不足任則病也 — "not knowing that knowledge cannot be relied on: that is the sickness."

道德經 ch. 71 (王弼本, with 王弼 note); silk ch. 36 (silk.txt:384–386, which follows A); 帛書本 page for A and B. Not in Guodian.

quoted

decision rule

To be above, put yourself below; to be in front, put yourself behind.

If you want to be above the people, you must put yourself below them in your words; if you want to be in front of them, you must put yourself behind them in your person. Then they do not feel your weight above them or harm from you in front, and because you do not contend, no one in the world can contend with you.

江海所以能為百谷王者，以其善下之，故能為百谷王。是以欲上民，必以言下之。欲先民，必以身後之。是以聖人處上而民不重，處前而民不害。是以天下樂推而不厭，以其不爭，故天下莫能與之爭。 — "Rivers and seas can be kings of the hundred valleys because they are good at being below them. So, wanting to be above the people, one must in speech put oneself below them; wanting to be ahead of the people, one must in person put oneself behind them. So the sage is above and the people do not feel the weight; he is in front and the people are not harmed. So the world gladly pushes him forward and does not tire of it. Because he does not contend, no one in the world can contend with him." Guodian 甲: 圣人之才（在）民前也，以身后之；其才（在）民上也，以言下之。其才（在）民上也，民弗厚也；其才（在）民前也，民弗害也。天下乐进而弗○（厌）。以其不静（争）也，古（故）天下莫能与之静（争）。

道德經 ch. 66 (王弼本); 郭店 甲 2–5; silk ch. 29 (silk.txt:319; A and B both). Guodian states it as what the sage does ("when he is in front of the people, he puts himself behind them"), without the 欲…必 "if you want…, you must" form that silk and WB have.

quoted

decision rule

Three treasures: compassion, frugality, not daring to be first.

Hold on to three treasures: compassion, frugality, and not daring to be first in the world. Compassion makes one able to be brave, frugality makes one able to be broad, and not daring to be first makes one able to become head of the vessels. To give these up and still be brave, broad and first is death.

我有三寶，持而保之。一曰慈，二曰儉，三曰不敢為天下先。慈故能勇，儉故能廣，不敢為天下先，故能成器長。今舍慈且勇，舍儉且廣，舍後且先，死矣！夫慈以戰則勝，以守則固。天將救之，以慈衛之。 — "I have three treasures; I hold and keep them. The first is compassion, the second frugality, the third not daring to be first in the world. Compassionate, one can be brave; frugal, one can be broad; not daring to be first in the world, one can become head of the vessels. Now to give up compassion and yet be brave, give up frugality and yet be broad, give up being behind and yet be first — that is death. With compassion, one wins in attack and holds firm in defence. Heaven will save him, guarding him with compassion."

道德經 ch. 67 (王弼本); silk ch. 32 (silk.txt:344–352: 一曰茲 二曰檢 … 天將建之 如以茲垣之). Not in Guodian.

quoted

mindset

The weak and soft overcome the hard and strong.

Reversal is how the Way moves; weakness is how the Way is used. The hard and strong go with death and the soft and weak with life. Nothing is softer than water, yet nothing does better at attacking the hard: everyone knows the weak beats the strong, and no one can practise it.

反者道之動，弱者道之用。 — "Reversal is the movement of the Way; weakness is the use of the Way." (ch. 40) · 故堅強者死之徒，柔弱者生之徒。是以兵強則不勝… 強大處下，柔弱處上。 — "So the hard and strong are companions of death, the soft and weak companions of life. So when an army is strong it does not win… The strong and great sit below; the soft and weak sit above." (ch. 76) · 天下莫柔弱於水，而攻堅強者，莫之能勝，其無以易之。弱之勝強，柔之勝剛，天下莫不知莫能行。是以聖人云：「受國之垢，是謂社稷主；受國不祥，是為天下王。」正言若反。 — "Nothing in the world is softer and weaker than water, yet for attacking the hard and strong nothing surpasses it; nothing can take its place. That the weak beats the strong and the soft beats the hard, everyone in the world knows and no one can practise. So the sage says: 'One who takes on the state's filth is called lord of its altars; one who takes on the state's misfortune is king of the world.' Straight words seem reversed." (ch. 78) Guodian 甲: 返也者，道○（动）也。溺（弱）也者，道之○（用）也。 (ch. 40)

道德經 chs. 40, 76, 78 (王弼本); 郭店 甲 37 (ch. 40 only; chs. 76 and 78 are not in Guodian). Silk ch. 4 (silk.txt:54), ch. 41 (:435), and ch. 43 (:455–457: 水之勝剛 弱之勝強 天下莫弗知 而莫能行也).

quoted

decision rule

What is to be shrunk must first be stretched.

What is to be shrunk must first be stretched; what is to be weakened must first be strengthened. What is to be discarded must first be raised (WB 廢/興; silk 去/與, "given to"), and what is to be taken must first be given. This is called subtle clarity (微明). The words do not say who does the stretching or what follows.

將欲歙之，必固張之；將欲弱之，必固強之；將欲廢之，必固興之；將欲奪之，必固與之。是謂微明。柔弱勝剛強。魚不可脫於淵，國之利器不可以示人。 — "About to shrink it, one must first stretch it; about to weaken it, one must first strengthen it; about to abolish it, one must first raise it; about to seize it, one must first give to it. This is called subtle clarity. The soft and weak beat the hard and strong. Fish must not leave the deep; the state's sharp instruments must not be shown to people." Silk A: 將欲拾之，必古張之；將欲弱之，□□強之；將欲去之，必古與之；將欲奪之，必古予之。是胃微明。柔弱勝強。魚不脫於瀟，邦利器不可以視人。

道德經 ch. 36 (王弼本); silk ch. 80 (silk.txt:882–886; A as quoted, from the 帛書本 page). Not in Guodian. 韓非子·喻老 reads it as strategy: 越王入宦於吳…故曰：「將欲翕之，必固張之」 and 晉獻公將欲襲虞，遺之以璧馬…故曰：「將欲取之，必固與之。」 That is Han Fei's application, not the text's words.

quoted

decision rule

Achieve the result and stop; use weapons when it cannot be avoided; mourn the victory.

One who helps a ruler by the Way does not use troops to force the world. The good one achieves the result and stops, and does not use it to take strength. He achieves it without vaunting, boasting or arrogance, and as something he could not avoid. Weapons are instruments of ill omen, used when there is no alternative; calm indifference is best, victory is not made beautiful, and a victory is treated with the rites of mourning.

以道佐人主者，不以兵強天下。其事好還。…善有果而已，不敢以取強。果而勿矜，果而勿伐，果而勿驕。果而不得已，果而勿強。 — "One who assists a ruler with the Way does not force the world with troops; such affairs tend to come back. … The good one has a result and that is all; he does not dare use it to take strength. Result, and no vaunting; result, and no boasting; result, and no arrogance; result, as something unavoidable; result, and no forcing." (ch. 30) · 兵者不祥之器，非君子之器，不得已而用之，恬淡為上。勝而不美，而美之者，是樂殺人。…戰勝，以喪禮處之。 — "Weapons are instruments of ill omen, not the gentleman's instruments; when it cannot be avoided he uses them, and calm indifference is best. He wins and does not find it beautiful; one who finds it beautiful delights in killing people. … A victory in war is handled with the rites of mourning." (ch. 31) Guodian 甲: 以○（道）差（佐）人○（主）者，不谷（欲）以兵强于天下。善者果而已，不以取强。果而弗发（伐），果而弗乔（骄），果而弗○（矜），是胃（谓）果而不强。 (ch. 30) · Guodian 丙: …得已而甬（用）之。○○为上，弗○（美）也。○〈美〉之，是乐杀人。…战○（胜）则以丧豊（礼）居之。 (ch. 31)

道德經 chs. 30, 31 (王弼本); 郭店 甲 6–8 (ch. 30), 丙 6–10 (ch. 31); silk chs. 74, 75 (silk.txt:806–833). WB has no commentary on ch. 31. 晁說之's postface in the sources file reports that Wang Bi took 佳兵者不祥之器…以喪禮處之 as 非老子之言, yet Guodian 丙 and both silk copies carry it.

quoted

decision rule

Do not display yourself; do not contend.

Bent, then whole; crooked, then straight; hollow, then full; worn, then new; little, then gaining; much, then confused. The sage does not display himself and so is clear, does not affirm himself and so stands out, does not boast and so has merit, and does not vaunt himself and so lasts; because he does not contend, no one in the world can contend with him.

曲則全，枉則直，窪則盈，敝則新，少則得，多則惑。是以聖人抱一為天下式。不自見故明，不自是故彰，不自伐故有功，不自矜故長。夫唯不爭，故天下莫能與之爭。 — "Bent, then whole; crooked, then straight; hollow, then full; worn, then new; little, then gained; much, then confused. So the sage embraces the one and is the world's model. Not displaying himself, he is clear; not affirming himself, he is distinguished; not boasting, he has merit; not vaunting, he lasts. Just because he does not contend, no one in the world can contend with him." (ch. 22) · 企者不立，跨者不行，自見者不明，自是者不彰，自伐者無功，自矜者不長。其在道也，曰餘食贅行。物或惡之，故有道者不處。 — "On tiptoe one does not stand; striding, one does not walk. Who displays himself is not clear; who affirms himself is not distinguished; who boasts has no merit; who vaunts does not last. In the Way these are called leftover food and superfluous action. Things may loathe them, so one who has the Way does not dwell in them." (ch. 24)

道德經 chs. 22, 24 (王弼本). Silk ch. 67 = received 22 (silk.txt:715–721, 執一以為天下牧) and silk ch. 66 = received 24 (:708–710, 炊者不立). The 明/彰 pairing swaps between silk A (不□視故明，不自見故章, one graph lost) and silk B (不自視故章，不自見也故明). Neither chapter is in Guodian.

quoted

mindset

The highest good is like water.

The highest good is like water: water benefits all things and does not contend (WB), and it settles where people dislike to be, so it is near the Way. Good in dwelling is the ground, in the heart depth, in giving benevolence (silk B: heaven), in speech trust, in governing order, in affairs ability, and in moving timing; because it does not contend, there is no blame.

上善若水。水善利萬物而不爭，處眾人之所惡，故幾於道。居善地，心善淵，與善仁，言善信，正善治，事善能，動善時。夫唯不爭，故無尤。 — "The highest good is like water. Water is good at benefiting the ten thousand things and does not contend; it settles where the crowd dislikes, and so it is near the Way. Dwelling: good is the ground. Heart: good is depth. Giving: good is benevolence. Speech: good is trust. Governing: good is order. Affairs: good is ability. Moving: good is timing. Just because it does not contend, there is no blame." Silk A: 上善治水﹦善利萬物而有靜…夫唯不靜，故無尤. Silk B: 上善如水﹦善利萬物而有爭…予善天，言善信…夫唯不爭，故無尤.

道德經 ch. 8 (王弼本); silk ch. 52 (silk.txt:550–554, a composite of A and B); 帛書本 page for A and B. Not in Guodian. Where WB has 而不爭, both silk copies have 而有—. A uses 靜 also for the closing 不爭, so the silk's sense at this point is unresolved (my reading).

quoted

mindset

Knowing yourself is clarity; overcoming yourself is strength.

Knowing others is cleverness; knowing yourself is clarity. Overcoming others takes force and overcoming yourself is strength; knowing what is enough is wealth, pressing on is will, not losing your place is lasting, and dying without perishing is long life.

知人者智，自知者明。勝人者有力，自勝者強。知足者富。強行者有志。不失其所者久。死而不亡者壽。 — "One who knows others is clever; one who knows himself is clear. One who overcomes others has force; one who overcomes himself is strong. One who knows what is enough is rich. One who presses on has will. One who does not lose his place lasts. One who dies and does not perish is long-lived."

道德經 ch. 33 (王弼本); silk ch. 77 (silk.txt:851–857: 知人者 知也 … 死不忘者 壽也; silk B 死而不忘者壽也, "dies and is not forgotten"). Not in Guodian.

quoted

mindset

The use is in what is not there.

The cart's use is in the empty space at the hub, the vessel's use in its hollow, and the room's use in the openings. So what is there gives benefit, and what is not there gives use. The words do not say to remove anything; that would be an application.

三十輻共一轂，當其無，有車之用。埏埴以為器，當其無，有器之用。鑿戶牖以為室，當其無，有室之用。故有之以為利，無之以為用。 — "Thirty spokes share one hub; in its nothing lies the cart's use. Clay is moulded into a vessel; in its nothing lies the vessel's use. Doors and windows are cut to make a room; in its nothing lies the room's use. So what is there makes for benefit; what is not there makes for use."

道德經 ch. 11 (王弼本); silk ch. 55 (silk.txt:583–589). Not in Guodian.

quoted

decision rule

When your time comes, ride out; when it does not, drift away.

A gentleman who gets his time rides out, and one who does not drifts away. The good merchant hides his goods deep as if he had none, and the gentleman of full virtue looks like a fool. Confucius is told to put away his arrogance and many desires, his airs and excessive aims, which do his person no good. Separately, as narrator, Sima Qian writes that Laozi's learning made hiding himself and namelessness its task, and that, seeing Zhou decline, he left.

老子曰：「子所言者，其人與骨皆已朽矣，獨其言在耳。且君子得其時則駕，不得其時則蓬累而行。吾聞之，良賈深藏若虛，君子盛德容貌若愚。去子之驕氣與多欲，態色與淫志，是皆無益於子之身。吾所以告子，若是而已。」 — "Laozi said: 'The men you speak of have rotted, they and their bones; only their words remain. And a gentleman, when he gets his time, rides out; when he does not get his time, he goes off like drifting tumbleweed. I have heard that a good merchant stores deep as if empty, and a gentleman of abundant virtue looks like a fool. Get rid of your arrogance and many desires, your airs and wanton ambition; none of these benefits your person. What I have to tell you is this, and only this.'" · Narrator: 老子修道德，其學以自隱無名為務。居周久之，見周之衰，乃遂去。 — "Laozi cultivated the Way and virtue; his learning made hiding himself and having no name its task. He lived long in Zhou; seeing Zhou's decline, he then left."

史記 卷63 老子韓非列傳 (sources/lao-tzu/史記_卷063.txt lines 13, 15). Line 21 is Sima Qian on the identification: 世莫知其然否.

attributed. The speech is Sima Qian's report of Laozi speaking to Confucius; the second part is the narrator's voice.

mindset

Where others take the front, take the rear; restraint as the rule.

Where everyone takes the front, he alone takes the rear, saying he takes on the world's reproach (variant: filth). Where everyone takes the solid, he alone takes the empty, and where everyone seeks good fortune, he alone stays bent and whole, saying "just escape blame". He takes depth as the root and restraint (約) as the rule, saying "the hard is broken, the sharp is blunted".

老耼曰：「知其雄，守其雌，爲天下谿。知其白，守其辱，爲天下谷。」人皆取先，己獨取後，曰：「受天下之詬（一作垢）。」人皆取實，己獨取虛。无藏也，故有餘，巋然而有餘。其行身也，徐而不費，无爲也而笑巧。人皆求福，己獨曲全，曰：「苟免於咎。」以深爲根，以約爲紀，曰：「堅則毀矣，銳則挫矣。」常寬容於物，不削於人。 — "Lao Dan said: 'Know the male, keep to the female, and be the world's ravine; know the white, keep to the disgraced, and be the world's valley.' Everyone takes the front; he alone takes the rear, saying: 'Take on the world's reproach' (variant: filth). Everyone takes the solid; he alone takes the empty. Hoarding nothing, he has more than enough, abundantly. In conducting himself he is slow and not wasteful; he does nothing and laughs at cleverness. Everyone seeks good fortune; he alone keeps bent and whole, saying: 'Just escape blame.' He takes depth as the root and restraint as the rule, saying: 'The hard is broken; the sharp is blunted.' He is always tolerant of things and does not pare away at people."

莊子·天下, the paragraph on 關尹 and 老耼 (zh.wikisource 莊子/天下).

attributed. This is the 天下 author's description, with sayings he attributes to Lao Dan. The paragraph opens with 關尹 and 老耼 together; the lines after 老耼曰 are read as about Lao Dan (my reading of the paragraph's order). 知其雄…為天下谷 matches 道德經 ch. 28; 受…詬/垢 echoes ch. 78's 受國之垢; 曲全 echoes ch. 22.
