Linus Torvalds

5 mindsets · 14 decision rules

Linus Benedict Torvalds (born 28 December 1969 in Helsinki, Finland; Swedish-speaking Finn, naturalised US citizen 2010) has been the creator and lead developer of the Linux kernel since 1991. He announced his "free operating system … just a hobby" for 386/486 AT clones on comp.os.minix on 25 August 1991 (Message-ID 1991Aug25.205708.9541@klaava.Helsinki.FI), released 1.0 on 14 March 1994, and relicensed the kernel under the GPLv2 after hearing Richard Stallman speak in the autumn of 1991 (Wikipedia, Linus Torvalds, citing Torvalds & Diamond, Just for Fun, and comp.os.minix; The early days of Linux, Lars Wirzenius, LWN). He worked at Transmeta from February 1997 to June 2003, then at OSDL and the Linux Foundation, and moved to Oregon in 2004. In 2005, after the BitKeeper dispute, he wrote Git starting 3 April 2005 and handed it to Junio Hamano by mid-2005; Git exists because "the Linux kernel developers needed a tool they could use to version the kernel". He wrote very little of the kernel himself — about 2% as of 2006 — and said in 2012 that his own contribution is now "mostly merging code written by others". What he kept was the last word: Documentation/process/submitting-patches.rst states, in the present tense, "Linus Torvalds is the final arbiter of all changes accepted into the Linux kernel", while noting that "very few patches go through Linus directly". He codified how he would exercise that power in prose rather than edicts — Documentation/process/management-style.rst ("This is a short document describing the preferred (or made up, depending on who you ask) management style for the linux kernel") and the much older coding-style.rst ("this is what goes for anything that I have to be able to maintain"). In September 2018, after The New Yorker reported on his years of abusive mailing-list mail, he replaced the kernel's Code of Conflict with a Code of Conduct, called his past attacks "unprofessional and uncalled for", took time off to work on how he responds to people, and returned to maintaining 4.19 in October 2018. Awards: 2012 Millennium Technology Prize, 2014 IEEE Computer Pioneer Award, 2018 IEEE Masaru Ibuka Consumer Electronics Award.

From the first research round; its Chinese quotes were checked, its other facts were not re-checked.

decision rule

A change that breaks what used to work for users is a kernel bug: fix it or revert it, in the kernel, and admit it.

If a change makes user programs break, the bug is in the kernel, not in the user program. The change must be fixed or reverted, and fixed in the kernel. When a regression happens, it is admitted and fixed instead of blamed on user space. If the kernel used to work for you, it continues to work for you. He says there have been exceptions, but "few and far between". For API breakage inside the kernel: whoever broke something fixes it too.

(English original)

  • "If a change results in user programs breaking, it's a bug in the kernel. We never EVER blame the user programs." … "WE DO NOT BREAK USERSPACE!"
  • "The first rule is: - we don't cause regressions and the corollary is that when regressions do occur, we admit to them and fix them, instead of blaming user space."
  • "If the kernel used to work for you, the rule is that it continues to work for you. There have been exceptions, but they are few and far between, and they generally have some major and fundamental reasons for having happened, that were basically entirely unavoidable, and people tried_hard to avoid them."
  • "But if something actually breaks, then the change must get fixed or reverted. And it gets fixed in the kernel."
  • "Nobody can say "I now broke the API you used, and now you need to fix it up". Whoever broke something gets to fix it too."

LKML, 23 Dec 2012, "Re: [Regression w/ patch] Media commit causes user space to misbahave (was: Re: Linux 3.8-rc1)", https://lkml.org/lkml/2012/12/23/75 · LKML, 26 Oct 2017, "Re: regression in 4.14-rc2 caused by apparmor: add base infastructure for socket mediation", https://lkml.iu.edu/hypermail/linux/kernel/1710.3/02474.html and …/1710.3/02487.html

quoted

mindset

Talk is cheap; show the code.

A claim that something can be built costs nothing to make; what he asks for is the code. In 2017 he did not accept a main pull request because its untested code "clearly didn't do what it claimed it did".

(English original)

  • "Talk is cheap. Show me the code." (his whole reply to Jamie Lokier's claim that the best of user-space and kernel threads could be combined "in less than 8kB per thread")
  • "untested code that clearly didn't do what it claimed it did, and which caused me to not even accept the main pull request"

LKML, 25 Aug 2000, "Re: SCO: "thread creation is about a thousand times faster than on native Linux"", https://lkml.org/lkml/2000/8/25/132 · LKML, 26 Oct 2017, same apparmor thread, https://lkml.iu.edu/hypermail/linux/kernel/1710.3/02507.html

quoted

decision rule

What counts as a regression is a user's breakage, not an ABI, a document or a test.

A regression is the kernel not giving the same end result with the same user space. The rule is about breaking a user's workflow. It is not about documented behaviour, about where the code lives, or about behaviour never changing. A test that now behaves differently is a warning sign, not by itself a regression. Changing an API is fine as long as nobody notices.

(English original)

  • "As far as the kernel is concerned, a regressions is THE KERNEL NOT GIVING THE SAME END RESULT WITH THE SAME USER SPACE." (2017)
  • "The rules about regressions have never been about any kind of documented behavior, or where the code lives. The rules about regressions are always about "breaks user workflow". Users are literally the only thing that matters." (2020)
  • "And our regression rule has never been "behavior doesn't change". That would mean that we could never make any changes at all." (2017)
  • "But if you have some random test that now behaves differently, it's not a regression. It's a warning sign, sure: tests are useful." (2024)
  • "You can make any changes to an API you like - as long as nobody notices." (2020/2021, see Gaps)

2017 line: LKML 26 Oct 2017, https://lkml.iu.edu/hypermail/linux/kernel/1710.3/02474.html (opened). The others: his mails as reproduced in Documentation/process/handling-regressions.rst, "Quotes from Linus about regression" (https://docs.kernel.org/process/handling-regressions.html), entries 2020-05-21, 2017-11-05, "2024-29-01" and 2021-05-21, each with its lore.kernel.org link (originals not opened).

quoted

decision rule

Avoid having to make the big decisions; the people who know the details should not need you to pick.

The aim is to avoid having to make decisions, at least the big and painful ones. If people you manage ask you to choose (a) or (b) on a technical matter, you are in trouble: they should know the details better than you, so you are not competent to decide it for them. If they don't know the details better than you, you are in the wrong job. Small, non-consequential decisions are fine. The job is to turn the big and painful ones into small things.

(English original) "The name of the game is to avoid having to make a decision. In particular, if somebody tells you "choose (a) or (b), we really need you to decide on this", you're in trouble as a manager. The people you manage had better know the details better than you, so if they come to you for a technical decision, you're screwed. You're clearly not competent to make that decision for them." … "So the name of the game is to avoid decisions, at least the big and painful ones. Making small and non-consequential decisions is fine, and makes you look like you know what you're doing, so what a kernel manager needs to do is to turn the big and painful ones into small things where nobody really cares."

Documentation/process/management-style.rst §1 "Decisions", https://docs.kernel.org/process/management-style.html. The same text is in LWN, 6 Oct 2004, "Linus on kernel management style", https://lwn.net/Articles/105375/

quoted. Authorship is by attribution only (see Gaps).

decision rule

A decision is big only if it can't be undone; avoid doing things that can't be undone.

What separates a big decision from a small one is whether you can fix it afterwards. Any decision can be made small by making sure that, if you were wrong (and you will be wrong), you can undo the damage by backtracking. So avoid doing things that can't be undone. Deleting the work is easy, but you may have irrevocably lost the trust of the engineer who did it, and then the decision was a big one after all.

(English original) "It helps to realize that the key difference between a big decision and a small one is whether you can fix your decision afterwards. Any decision can be made small by just always making sure that if you were wrong (and you will be wrong), you can always undo the damage later by backtracking." … "Thus the key to avoiding big decisions becomes to just avoiding to do things that can't be undone. Don't get ushered into a corner from which you cannot escape." … "while the actual work was easy enough to undo by just deleting it, you may have irrevocably lost the trust of that engineer. And remember: "irrevocable" was what we tried to avoid in the first place, and your decision ended up being a big one after all."

management-style.rst §1 "Decisions"; LWN 2004 (as #4)

quoted. Authorship is by attribution only (see Gaps).

decision rule

Let people smarter than you make the decisions; prod, don't push too hard.

Take advantage of smart people: they can make your decisions for you. When you find somebody smarter than you, coast along, and your job becomes saying "Sounds like a good idea - go wild" or "That sounds good, but what about xxx?". Greatness in one area does not necessarily carry over to others. You may prod people in a direction, which is not irreversible because people drift back to what they are good at, but don't push too hard.

(English original) "Some people react badly to smart people. Others take advantage of them. Make sure that you, as a kernel maintainer, are in the second group. Suck up to them, because they are the people who will make your job easier. In particular, they'll be able to make your decisions for you, which is what the game is all about." … "So when you find somebody smarter than you are, just coast along. Your management responsibilities largely become ones of saying "Sounds like a good idea - go wild", or "That sounds good, but what about xxx?"." … "One thing to look out for is to realize that greatness in one area does not necessarily translate to other areas. So you might prod people in specific directions, but let's face it, they might be good at what they do, and suck at everything else. The good news is that people tend to naturally gravitate back to what they are good at, so it's not like you are doing something irreversible when you do prod them in some direction, just don't push too hard."

management-style.rst §3 "People II - the Good Kind"; LWN 2004

quoted. Authorship is by attribution only (see Gaps).

mindset

Say up front that you may be wrong; give people critical thinking, not confidence.

Admit up front that you don't know. Tell people ahead of time that your decision is preliminary and might be wrong, keep the right to change your mind, and make sure they know it. If the people doing the work aren't sure their work is a good idea, don't encourage them by promising it will be included; make them think twice before a big endeavour. The best thing a manager can do is give them a healthy dose of critical thinking about what they do, not confidence. And you are one of the idiots too.

(English original, in source order) "Happily, both of these reasons can be mitigated effectively by just admitting up-front that you don't have a friggin' clue, and telling people ahead of the fact that your decision is purely preliminary, and might be the wrong thing. You should always reserve the right to change your mind, and make people very aware of that." … "After all, if they aren't certain whether it's a good idea, you sure as hell shouldn't encourage them by promising them that what they work on will be included. Make them at least think twice before they embark on a big endeavor." … "The best thing you can do as a manager is not to instill confidence, but rather a healthy dose of critical thinking on what they do." … (§3) "While it turns out that most people are idiots, the corollary to that is sadly that you are one too"

management-style.rst §1 "Decisions", §3 "People II - the Good Kind"; LWN 2004

quoted. Authorship is by attribution only (see Gaps).

decision rule

When it isn't clear which of two approaches is better, ask "can't we just do both?"

Another way to avoid a decision is to ask "can't we just do both?". If it is not clear which approach is better, the people involved will eventually figure it out. Sometimes both teams give up. He reads that as usually a sign that both projects had something wrong with them, and that they couldn't decide because both were wrong.

(English original) "Btw, another way to avoid a decision is to plaintively just whine "can't we just do both?" and look pitiful. Trust me, it works. If it's not clear which approach is better, they'll eventually figure it out. The answer may end up being that both teams get so frustrated by the situation that they just give up." … "That may sound like a failure, but it's usually a sign that there was something wrong with both projects, and the reason the people involved couldn't decide was that they were both wrong."

management-style.rst §1 "Decisions"; LWN 2004

quoted. Authorship is by attribution only (see Gaps).

mindset

Design the code around the data, not the other way round.

He favours designing code around the data rather than the reverse, and gives it as one reason git worked. He claims the difference between a bad programmer and a good one is whether they treat their code or their data structures as more important.

(English original) "In fact, I'm a huge proponent of designing your code around the data, rather than the other way around, and I think it's one of the reasons git has been fairly successful ()." … "() I will, in fact, claim that the difference between a bad programmer and a good one is whether he considers his code or his data structures more important. Bad programmers worry about the code. Good programmers worry about data structures and their relationships."

git mailing list, 27 Jul 2006, "Re: Licensing and the library version of git", Message-ID Pine.LNX.4.64.0607270936200.4168@g5.osdl.org, https://marc.info/?l=git&m=115401850825206&w=2 (also LWN Quote of the week, 29 Jul 2006, https://lwn.net/Articles/193244/)

quoted

mindset

Good code: see the problem differently so the special case becomes the normal case.

Sometimes you can see a problem in a different way and rewrite it so that a special case goes away and becomes the normal case, and he calls that good code. The sign of people he wants to work with is good taste, which is about seeing the big patterns and knowing by instinct the right way to do things.

(English original, spoken; about two ways to remove an entry from a singly linked list) "I want you to understand that sometimes you can see a problem in a different way and rewrite it so that a special case goes away and becomes the normal case. And that's good code." … "To me, the sign of people I really want to work with is that they have good taste" … "Good taste is about really seeing the big patterns and kind of instinctively knowing what's the right way to do things."

TED2016, "The mind behind Linux" (interview with Chris Anderson), transcript at https://www.ted.com/talks/linus_torvalds_the_mind_behind_linux/transcript

quoted (spoken, as TED's transcript gives it)

decision rule

A pull must tell him what he is pulling and why, as a record that will last; anything odd or late must be explained.

To him, the message is the important part. He wants to understand what he is pulling and why he should pull it. The message becomes the merge message, so it must also make sense as a historical record. Anything odd belongs in the explanation. If you touch files you don't maintain, explain why; he will see it in the diffstat anyway, and if it isn't mentioned he gets extra suspicious. For anything sent after the merge window, or fixes that look scary, explain what it does, why, and the timing.

(English original) "Anyway, at least to me, the important part is the message. I want to understand what I'm pulling, and why I should pull it. I also want to use that message as the message for the merge, so it should not just make sense to me, but make sense as a historical record too. Note that if there is something odd about the pull request, that should very much be in the explanation. If you're touching files that you don't maintain, explain why. I will see it in the diffstat anyway, and if you didn't mention it, I'll just be extra suspicious. And when you send me new stuff after the merge window (or even bug-fixes, but ones that look scary), explain not just what they do and why they do it, but explain the timing. What happened that this didn't go through the merge window.."

LKML, 14 Nov 2017, "Re: git pull", https://lkml.iu.edu/hypermail/linux/kernel/1711.1/04939.html (also reproduced in Documentation/maintainer/pull-requests.rst, "As said by Linus")

quoted

decision rule

Clean history: rebase your own private work, never other people's history; merge only for a reason.

People can, and probably should, rebase their own private trees, which is cleanup. Never rebase other people's history, which destroys it. The rule is about history, not code: a patch you applied yourself is your history. Once you have published your history, it is no longer private. Don't push out work that is still in the rebase phase. Don't merge upstream code at random points, and have a reason for merging downstream work. He won't pull from a tree whose log is full of random merges of his tree.

(English original) "I want clean history, but that really means (a) clean and (b) history. People can (and probably should) rebase their private trees (their own work). That's a cleanup. But never other peoples code. That's a "destroy history"" … "You must never EVER destroy other peoples history. You must not rebase commits other people did." … "Notice that this really is about other peoples history, not about other peoples code." … "once you've published your history in some public site, other people may be using it, and so now it's clearly not your private history any more." … "Don't expose your crap. This means: if you're still in the "git rebase" phase, you don't push it out." … "Don't merge upstream code at random points." … "Slightly more complex version: "Always have a reason for merging downstream stuff"." … "But if I see a lot of "Merge branch 'linus'" in your logs, I'm not going to pull from you, because your tree has obviously had random crap in it that shouldn't be there."

"Re: [git pull] drm-next", to Dave Airlie, 29 Mar 2009, Message-ID alpine.LFD.2.00.0903291409030.3994@localhost.localdomain, as published at https://lwn.net/Articles/328438/

quoted

mindset

Start small, for an immediate need; don't push your "vision" too hard on the project.

Don't set out to build a large project. Start with a small, trivial one and don't expect it to get large; expecting that leads to over-design, or to being scared off. Think about the details, not a big picture: if it doesn't solve a fairly immediate need, it is almost certainly over-designed. Projects have a life of their own, so don't enforce your "vision" too strongly. You are usually wrong anyway, so be willing to take input, change direction and admit mistakes.

(English original) "Nobody should start to undertake a large project. You start with a small trivial project, and you should never expect it to get large. If you do, you'll just overdesign and generally think it is more important than it likely is at that stage. Or worse, you might be scared away by the sheer size of the work you envision. So start small, and think about the details. Don't think about some big picture and fancy design. If it doesn't solve some fairly immediate need, it's almost certainly over-designed." … "projects have a life of their own, and you should not try to enforce your "vision" too strongly on them. Most often you're wrong anyway, and if you're not flexible and willing to take input from others (and willing to change direction when it turned out your vision was flawed), you'll never get anything good done. In other words, be willing to admit your mistakes" · TED2016: "I am not a visionary. I do not have a five-year plan. I'm an engineer." … "But I'm looking at the ground, and I want to fix the pothole that's right in front of me before I fall in."

Linux Times email interview by Preston St. Pierre, posted 25 Oct 2004 ("Linus Torvalds: 'Desktop Market has already started'"), Wayback capture https://web.archive.org/web/20041106193140/http://www.linuxtimes.net/modules.php?name=News&file=article&sid=145 · TED2016 transcript (as #10)

quoted

decision rule

Patches go to the subsystem maintainer; he trusts the maintainers he pulls from and avoids being the throttle.

Patches go to the subsystem maintainer, and very few go through him directly. People are told to avoid sending him email even though he is the final arbiter. When he pulls from maintainers, the attention he gives varies: sometimes he looks quite closely, but as a general rule he trusts them not to send bad patches. In his own words in 2005, he can process a hundred emailed patches almost as easily as one "as long as I trust the maintainer". If no parallel-merge tool could be found soon, he would distribute the merging over a few people rather than be the throttle himself.

(English original)

  • Doc: "Linus Torvalds is the final arbiter of all changes accepted into the Linux kernel. … He gets a lot of e-mail, and, at this point, very few patches go through Linus directly, so typically you should do your best to -avoid- sending him e-mail."
  • Doc: "The amount of attention that Linus pays to specific patches received in a pull operation varies. It is clear that, sometimes, he looks quite closely. But, as a general rule, Linus trusts the subsystem maintainers to not send bad patches upstream."
  • His 2005 words: "I can process a hundred emails almost as easily as one, as long as I trust the maintainer (which, when it's used as a BK replacement, I obviously do)." … "at least try to distribute the merging out over a few people rather than making me be the throttle."

Documentation/process/submitting-patches.rst "Select the recipients for your patch" · Documentation/process/2.Process.rst §2.3 "How patches get into the Kernel" · LKML, 7 Apr 2005, "Re: Kernel SCM saga..", https://lkml.iu.edu/hypermail/linux/kernel/0504.0/1826.html

the two doc passages are attributed (third person, not his); the 2005 lines are quoted.

decision rule

Take the blame, best of all for someone else; tell the one who really screwed up in private.

When things go wrong, take the blame, and the best way is to take it for someone else. Then let the developer who really screwed up (if you can find them) know in private. That way they can avoid it next time, they know they owe you one, and they are likely the person who can fix it. Taking the blame is part of what makes people trust you.

(English original) "Which brings us to the best way of taking the blame: do it for someone else. You'll feel good for taking the fall, they'll feel good about not getting blamed" … "Then make the developer who really screwed up (if you can find them) know in private that they screwed up. Not just so they can avoid it in the future, but so that they know they owe you one. And, perhaps even more importantly, they're also likely the person who can fix it." … "Taking the blame is also why you get to be manager in the first place. It's part of what makes people trust you"

management-style.rst §4 "Placing blame"; LWN 2004

quoted. Authorship is by attribution only (see Gaps).

decision rule

Don't hide the problem in politeness; never be sanctimonious; apologise. In 2018 he apologised for his personal attacks.

Don't be too polite or subtle, because politeness can end up hiding the problem; make the point bluntly. Some humour can soften both the bluntness and the moralizing. Don't call people d*ckheads (at least not in public), and learn to apologise when you do. Worse than that is saying it in a sanctimonious voice, which people may not give you the chance to apologise for. Alienating people counts as "not reversible". In 2018 he wrote that his flippant attacks in email, especially the personal ones, were unprofessional and uncalled for, that this was not OK, and that he needed to change his behaviour.

(English original) "Similarly, don't be too polite or subtle about things. Politeness easily ends up going overboard and hiding the problem, and as they say, "On the internet, nobody can hear you being subtle". Use a big blunt object to hammer the point in, because you can't really depend on people getting your point otherwise. Some humor can help pad both the bluntness and the moralizing." … "don't call people dckheads (at least not in public)" / "learn how to apologize when you forgot rule (1)" … "There's one thing people hate even more than being called "dckhead", and that is being called a "d*ckhead" in a sanctimonious voice. The first you can apologize for, the second one you won't really get the chance." … "It turns out that alienating people is fairly easy, and un-alienating them is hard. Thus "alienating" immediately falls under the heading of "not reversible"" · 2018: "My flippant attacks in emails have been both unprofessional and uncalled for. Especially at times when I made it personal. In my quest for a better patch, this made sense to me. I know now this was not OK and I am truly sorry." … "hey, I need to change some of my behavior"

management-style.rst §2 "People", §5 "Things to avoid"; LWN 2004 · LKML, 16 Sep 2018, "Linux 4.19-rc4 released, an apology, and a maintainership note", https://lkml.org/lkml/2018/9/16/167

quoted (management-style authorship by attribution only, see Gaps; the 2018 mail is his)

decision rule

For code he has to maintain: short functions that do one thing, shallow nesting, comments that say what and not how.

These are his rules for code he has to maintain. He won't force them on anybody else, but would prefer them there too. Functions should be short and do one thing. If you need more than 3 levels of indentation, fix your program. Local variables shouldn't exceed 5–10, because "maybe you'd like to understand what you did 2 weeks from now". Comments should say what the code does, not how. A formatting tool is not a fix for bad programming.

(English original) "Coding style is very personal, and I won't force my views on anybody, but this is what goes for anything that I have to be able to maintain, and I'd prefer it for most other things too. Please at least consider the points made here." … "if you need more than 3 levels of indentation, you're screwed anyway, and should fix your program." … "Functions should be short and sweet, and do just one thing." … "Another measure of the function is the number of local variables. They shouldn't exceed 5-10, or you're doing something wrong." … "You know you're brilliant, but maybe you'd like to understand what you did 2 weeks from now." … "Generally, you want your comments to tell WHAT your code does, not HOW." … "But remember: "indent" is not a fix for bad programming."

Documentation/CodingStyle in the Linux 2.0 release (1996), chapters 1, 4, 5 and 6 (https://cdn.kernel.org/pub/linux/kernel/v2.0/linux-2.0.tar.gz). The same sentences are in today's Documentation/process/coding-style.rst, opening and §1, §6, §8, §9.

quoted, first person ("anything that I have to be able to maintain"). Authorship is by attribution, not by signature (see Gaps).

decision rule

Quantify the claimed win and state its costs; the description must stand alone.

Describe the problem that motivated the patch and its impact on users. If you claim improvements in performance, memory, stack footprint or binary size, include numbers that back them up. Also describe the expected downsides, so the reviewer can weigh costs against benefits. Every submission or resubmission carries its complete description, not just "version N", so that it is self-contained.

(English original) "Describe your problem. Whether your patch is a one-line bug fix or 5000 lines of a new feature, there must be an underlying problem that motivated you to do this work." … "Quantify optimizations and trade-offs. If you claim improvements in performance, memory consumption, stack footprint, or binary size, include numbers that back them up. But also describe non-obvious costs." … "Describe the expected downsides of your optimization so that the reviewer can weigh costs against benefits." … "Don't just say that this is version N of the patch (series)." … "I.e., the patch (series) and its description should be self-contained."

Documentation/process/submitting-patches.rst "Describe your changes", https://docs.kernel.org/process/submitting-patches.html

attributed: kernel process documentation, not shown to be his words. He is named in the same document as the final arbiter.

decision rule

One logical change per patch, each one buildable; send a long series about 15 at a time.

Put each logical change in its own patch, and keep a single change across many files in one patch. Each patch should be easy to understand, verifiable, and justifiable on its own merits. In a series, the kernel should build and run after each patch, because git bisect may split the series anywhere. If you cannot condense the set, post say 15 or so at a time and wait for review and integration.

(English original) "Separate each logical change into a separate patch." … "On the other hand, if you make a single change to numerous files, group those changes into a single patch." … "The point to remember is that each patch should make an easily understood change that can be verified by reviewers. Each patch should be justifiable on its own merits." … "take special care to ensure that the kernel builds and runs properly after each patch in the series. Developers using git bisect to track down a problem can end up splitting your patch series at any point; they will not thank you if you introduce bugs in the middle." … "If you cannot condense your patch set into a smaller set of patches, then only post say 15 or so at a time and wait for review and integration."
